claims.text: An integrated machine-learning free-energy framework can capture vibrational, configurational, and anharmonic contributions for both solid and fluid phases at fusion conditions with high fidelity.
The proposed framework can significantly reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
A method applicable to elemental and binary systems can be extended to compositionally complex high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states near fusion.
An actively learned machine-learning interatomic potential can be trained on a strategically sampled set of ab initio data.
Combining active learning with effective-temperature scaling can approximate the free-energy contributions needed to replace full ab initio MD and TOR-TILD calculations.
Established scaling laws describe lattice distortions and chemical fluctuations at or just above fusion temperatures in elemental, binary, and selected high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions and chemical fluctuations in fusion-relevant solid and liquid configurations can be captured by the machine-learned potential.
Static interatomic-length disorder and temperature-driven dynamic lattice distortion can be related through an effective-temperature scaling law in high-entropy-alloy models.
Selected ab initio training points can accurately sample the vibrational and configurational free energies relevant to fusion.
Active learning and effective-temperature scaling reduce the amount of costly simulation sampling required to approximate free-energy landscapes.
The proposed machine-learning framework will retain the anharmonic free-energy contributions required at fusion conditions.
The proposed machine-learning framework will retain electron-vibration coupling contributions.
Solid-liquid free-energy differences predicted by the framework will agree with full ab initio MD to within approximately 5–10%.
Fusion temperatures and entropy contributions predicted by the framework will agree with full ab initio MD to within approximately 5–10%.
The framework will reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
Explicit ab initio workflows are computationally demanding for multicomponent alloys.
TOR-TILD is especially computationally intensive for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The framework will remain valid for elemental, binary, and moderately complex high-entropy-alloy systems near fusion.
Transferability outside the stated material classes or at extreme conditions may be limited.
Deviation greater than 5–10% in solid-liquid free-energy differences or fusion temperatures, or failure to capture the required entropy contributions, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
